In mathematics and theoretical computer science, a '''splicing language''' is a [[formal language]] which formalizes the action of [[gene splicing]] in [[molecular biology]]. Splicing languages have a variety of definitions based on the form of ''splicing rules'' allowed, which describe how one may "cut" and "paste together" strings from the language to obtain new strings. In all of them, given an initial language <math>I</math> over a finite alphabet <math>\Sigma</math> and a set of splicing rules <math>R</math>, a splicing language is the smallest language containing <math>I</math> which is closed under applying any splicing rule <math>r\in R</math>.

The original definition of a splicing language was given by Head in 1987.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Head |first=T |date=1987 |title=Formal language theory and DNA: An analysis of the generative capacity of specific recombinant behaviors |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1016/S0092-8240(87)90018-8 |journal=Bulletin of Mathematical Biology |language=en |volume=49 |issue=6 |pages=737–759 |doi=10.1016/S0092-8240(87)90018-8|doi-broken-date=9 October 2025 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Later on, alternative and inequivalent definitions were provided by [[Gheorghe Păun|Păun]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Păun |first1=Gheorghe |last2=Rozenberg |first2=Grzegorz |last3=Salomaa |first3=Arto |date=1996-11-20 |title=Computing by splicing |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304397596000825 |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |volume=168 |issue=2 |pages=321–336 |doi=10.1016/S0304-3975(96)00082-5 |issn=0304-3975|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and Pixton.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pixton |first=Dennis |date=1996-08-13 |title=Regularity of splicing languages |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0166-218X%2895%2900079-7 |journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics |volume=69 |issue=1 |pages=101–124 |doi=10.1016/0166-218X(95)00079-7 |issn=0166-218X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The class of languages generated by Head splicing is strictly contained in that of those generated by Păun splicing, which is in turn strictly contained in that of those generated by Pixton splicing.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bonizzoni |first1=P. |last2=Ferretti |first2=C. |last3=Mauri |first3=G. |last4=Zizza |first4=R. |date=2001-09-30 |title=Separating some splicing models |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0020019001001399 |journal=Information Processing Letters |volume=79 |issue=6 |pages=255–259 |doi=10.1016/S0020-0190(01)00139-9 |issn=0020-0190|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Definition==
The following definition is that of a Păun splicing system,<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Păun |first1=Gheorghe |last2=Rozenberg |first2=Grzegorz |last3=Salomaa |first3=Arto |date=1998 |title=DNA Computing |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-662-03563-4  |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-03563-4|isbn=978-3-642-08388-4 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> which is most common:

Let <math>\Sigma</math> be a finite alphabet and <math>I\subseteq\Sigma^*</math> a language.  A '''splicing rule''' is a quadruple <math>r=(u_1,v_1,u_2,v_2)\in(\Sigma^*)^4</math> (often written <math>r=(u_1,v_1;u_2,v_2)</math>). For <math>w_1,w_2\in\Sigma^*</math> and a splicing rule <math>r=(u_1,v_1;u_2,v_2)\in(\Sigma^*)^4</math>, we write <math>(w_1,w_2)\vdash_r z</math> if <math>w_1=x_1u_1v_1y_1</math>, <math>w_2=x_2u_2v_2y_2</math>, and <math>z=x_1u_1v_2y_2</math>. If <math>R</math> is a set of splicing rules over <math>\Sigma</math>, we say that <math>\sigma=(\Sigma,R)</math> is an H-scheme and define the action of <math>\sigma</math> on <math>I</math> to be <math>\sigma(I)=\{z\in\Sigma^*:\exists w_1,w_2\in I\text{ s.t. }(w_1,w_2)\vdash_r z\text{ }\forall r\in R\}</math>. Now, inductively, let <math>\sigma^0(I)=I</math> and <math>\sigma^{i+1}(I)=\sigma(\sigma^i(I))</math>. <math>\sigma^*(I)=\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb{Z}^+_0}\sigma^i(I)</math> is the splicing language generated by the '''H-system''' <math>H=(\Sigma,I,R)</math>. That is, the smallest language containing <math>I</math> and closed under applications of any <math>r\in R</math>.

A rule set <math>R</math> is '''reflexive''' if <math>(u_1,v_1;u_2,v_2)\in R</math> implies that <math>(u_1,v_1;u_1,v_1),(u_2,v_2;u_2,v_2)\in R</math>.  A rule set  <math>R</math> is '''symmetric''' if <math>(u_1,v_1;u_2,v_2)\in R</math> implies that <math>(u_2,v_2;u_1,v_1)\in R</math>. A splicing language is called reflexive (resp. symmetric) if it is generated by a reflexive (resp. symmetric) H-system.

== Results and Examples ==
A non-example of a splicing language is <math>(aa)^*</math>, whereas <math>b(aa)^*</math> is a splicing language. In fact, if <math>L</math> is a regular language on the alphabet <math>\Sigma</math>, and <math>b</math> is a letter not in <math>\Sigma</math>, then the language <math>bL=\{bw:w\in L\}</math> is a splicing language.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Anderson |first=James A. |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/automata-theory-with-modern-applications/C209E9807ED2EBB5F072A9861D33CDF8 |title=Automata Theory with Modern Applications |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-84887-9 |location=Cambridge |doi=10.1017/cbo9780511607202}}</ref>

All splicing languages generated by a finite initial language and finite rule set are [[Regular language|regular]].<ref name=":0" />

It is [[Decision problem|decidable]] whether or not a regular language is a splicing language<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kari |first1=Lila |last2=Kopecki |first2=Steffen |date=2017-03-01 |title=Deciding whether a regular language is generated by a splicing system |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022000016300940 |journal=Journal of Computer and System Sciences |volume=84 |pages=263–287 |doi=10.1016/j.jcss.2016.10.001 |issn=0022-0000|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and whether or not it is reflexive.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Head |first1=Tom |last2=Pixton |first2=Dennis |last3=Goode |first3=Elizabeth |date=2003 |editor-last=Hagiya |editor-first=Masami |editor2-last=Ohuchi |editor2-first=Azuma |chapter=Splicing Systems: Regularity and Below |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-36440-4_23 |title=DNA Computing |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=2568 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=262–268 |doi=10.1007/3-540-36440-4_23 |isbn=978-3-540-36440-5|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> Both algorithms make use of the decidability of whether or not a splicing rule '''respects''' a regular language, meaning that the language is closed under splicing by that rule.

Every regular splicing language contains a '''constant''', which is a word <math>c\in\Sigma^*</math> such that <math>u_1cv_1,u_2cv_2\in L</math> implies that <math>u_1cv_2,u_2cv_1\in L</math> for any <math>u_1,v_1,u_2,v_2\in\Sigma^*</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bonizzoni |first1=Paola |last2=Jonoska |first2=Nataša |date=2015-06-01 |title=Existence of constants in regular splicing languages |journal=Information and Computation |volume=242 |pages=340–353 |doi=10.1016/j.ic.2015.04.001 |issn=0890-5401 |pmc=4866503 |pmid=27185985}}</ref>

<math>b(aa)^*\cup(aa)^*b\cup(aa)^*</math> is a reflexive splicing language which is not symmetric. It is also generated by a finite splicing system.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Goode |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Pixton |first2=Dennis |date=2007-04-15 |title=Recognizing splicing languages: Syntactic monoids and simultaneous pumping |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X06004562 |journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics |volume=155 |issue=8 |pages=989–1006 |doi=10.1016/j.dam.2006.10.006 |issn=0166-218X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math>a^*ba^*ba^*\cup a^*ba^*\cup a^*</math> is a splicing language generated by a finite splicing system which is neither reflexive nor symmetric.<ref name=":1" />
